title: Navigation for an education product
excerpt: Use labels teachers and parents already say, and one path that starts a class or a trial. Department names waste the little time they have.
alt: Skyscrapers photographed from street level against a pale sky, a skyline that only helps if you know which door to enter.
caption: Skyscrapers from street level against a pale sky. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Which labels should an education site use?
faqs.answer: Words a teacher or parent would text to a friend. For teachers, for families, pricing, and start a class or start a trial. Platform, resources, and ecosystem are department names. They waste a short visit.

faqs.question: How should log in be treated?
faqs.answer: As a real job for people who already began, in a quieter treatment than the start. If a new parent hits log in first and stalls, the emphasis is wrong. The first visit should lead to the lesson, not to an account they do not have.

faqs.question: What belongs in the phone menu?
faqs.answer: The same jobs, in the same order, with type large enough to read outdoors. Do not add a newsletter, a video, or a second taxonomy. A teacher between classes will not study a large menu of every grade.

markdown:
Education product website navigation is a map of jobs, not a list of departments. For a teacher or a parent with little time, the labels should match words they already use, and one path should start a class or a trial.

They will not study your information architecture. They will tap the word that sounds like their life. If the word is wrong, they leave, often before they see the lesson you were proud of.

## A map of jobs

The jobs are simple. See the learning moment. Choose the version that fits, family or class or school. Understand what it costs. Start. Trust the people if they are unsure. Those jobs are the bar. A journal, a manifesto, and a "platform" link are not jobs for this buyer. They are places the team stores extra writing.

[The W3C's overview of WCAG](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) describes a usable interface as perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. Navigation is where operable and understandable show up first. Each link needs a purpose. The same label should reach the same place from the header and the footer. A teacher using a keyboard in a classroom, or a parent on a phone with the brightness up, should be able to read the words and hit them.

Name the product's doors in their language. For teachers. For families. Pricing. Start a class, or Start a trial. About, if the about page truly says who edits the lessons. Log in, for people who already began, placed so it does not compete with starting. Log in is a job. It is not the main job of a first visit. Do not style it as the primary action.

Do not organize the bar by your internal teams. Curriculum. Growth. Community. Partnerships. A parent does not have a job called partnerships. A teacher might, and they still came to see if the activity fits a period. Give partnerships a page if schools ask for it, and a label that says Schools, not a department.

## Words they already use

Say the labels the way they would say them to a friend. "Open the teacher page." "Look at pricing." "Start the trial." If you would be embarrassed to text that sentence, change the label. "Explore learning journeys" is an embarrassed sentence. It also takes longer to read, and this reader does not have longer.

Keep each label to one or two words. The bar is not a second headline. The homepage can say the learning moment. The nav can point at it. When you need a sentence to explain a label, the label is a page that has not been named, or a page that should not be in the bar.

Match the labels to the pages. If the page says "Start a class," the nav should not say "Get started" or "Join." One verb, used everywhere, is how a tired person learns the site in a single pass. Synonyms feel creative in a workshop and feel like three products in a hallway.

For teachers and For families are better than Solutions and Individuals, if those are the two real doors. Tutors can have a label if the offer is different in a way the page explains. If tutors use the family product, do not give them a nav item that leads to a thin duplicate. Send them to the door that matches the signup they will actually get.

## One path to a class or a trial

One item is the action. If teachers and families start in different places, the bar can show the door they came for, and the page can offer the specific button. What you should not do is place Start a class, Book a demo, Talk to sales, and Sign up free in the same bar. That is four products shouting. Pick the primary start for the buyer this page is for. Put the other starts inside the right door, labeled honestly.

The action should land on a short start, not on a ten-field form and not on a calendar with no context. A teacher should see what a class requires. A parent should see what a trial includes, including whether a card is needed. If the destination is not ready, the nav item is a promise you will break in the next three seconds. Fix the destination first.

Log in should not wear the same emphasis as the start. Returning teachers need it. New parents should not think the only path is an account they already failed to create. Place log in in the corner or the footer in a quieter treatment. Test with someone who has never seen the product. Ask them where they would begin. If they choose log in and then stall, your emphasis is wrong.

A chat widget that covers the action is a second navigation system. It asks a parent to explain the lesson to a bot before they have seen the lesson. Remove it from the first visit, or park it where it cannot cover Start a trial. The path you designed is the support, until they are actually stuck inside a class.

## How many items

Four or five is enough. For teachers. For families. Pricing. About. The start. Schools can replace one of these if school is the real business, or live under a footer link until you can staff the page. A blog can live in the footer unless a specific article is how teachers decide. Do not put Resources in the bar as a drawer of everything you could not name.

Drop the items that serve you. Careers, when you are not hiring. A press page. A second logo that links to a parent company. Social icons in the header. A search box on a small site. These can exist in the footer in small type. They should not sit beside the learning moment.

Skip the mega-menu. A panel that opens onto every grade, every subject, every PDF, and a featured quote is a second homepage. If teachers need to filter by grade, that filter belongs on the teacher page, not in the global bar. The bar answers "which door." The page answers "which lesson."

Remove the logo mentally and read the row. Could a substitute teacher understand it? Could a grandparent? If a label only makes sense after a brand video, it is not a label. Replace it with the job.

## On a phone, between classes

Teachers will open the link between classes. Parents will open it in a pickup line. The menu has to be the same jobs in the same order as the wide screen. A different phone taxonomy is a second site. You will forget to update one of them, and the buyer will land in the wrong start.

The start action should be tappable inside the menu and visible on the first screen. Do not bury Start a class under a newsletter, an app-store badge, and a paragraph about your mission. App-store badges can sit after they know what the lesson is. The store is not the navigation. It is a destination you earn.

Type in the open menu should be large, with real contrast, in a weight you can read outdoors. [WCAG's point](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) is that text has to be perceivable and controls have to be operable. A pale, thin menu fails that on a sunny bench, which is a normal place to decide about a child's afternoon. Hit targets should be easy with a thumb. Do not pack twelve links into the sheet.

Do not animate the menu into a performance. A teacher with one minute does not want a transition. Open, show the words, close when they choose. If a video is playing under the menu, pause it. The learning moment can wait a second. The labels cannot compete with motion.

## Labels to retire

Retire Platform, Solution, Ecosystem, Resources, Insights, Community, and Get Started, unless Get Started is truly the only start and the page says whether it is a class or a trial. Retire any label that exists so a synonym can rank. One destination, one word. Link that word from the homepage and the proof pages.

Retire a label you cannot staff. If Schools opens onto a form nobody answers, remove Schools until a person owns the reply. If About is still a myth, fix it or take it out of the bar. Navigation is a contract with a person who has little time. Breaking it teaches them that the product will break its promises too.

Retire clever icons with no text. A book, a hat, a spark. You have room for the word. The word is the respect. Icons can support a word. They should not replace it for a parent who will not guess.

When the labels are true, the pictures under them have to show the learning moment those labels promised. [Photography direction for an education product](/blog/photography-direction-for-an-education-product) is the next piece. A For teachers label that opens onto a dashboard of badges is a broken contract, even if the menu itself is short.

If you want the map and the pages brought into one site, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). Bring the labels you are using now, including Resources. The useful result is a shorter bar and one path that starts a class or a trial.
